reminder: The category of descent data has, as objects, local objects on a cover with gluing isomorphisms that satisfy the cocycle condition.
definition: Let $F$ be a [fibered category](c:grothendieck-fibration) over a [site](c:grothendieck-site) and let $\{U_i\to U\}$ be a covering family. A descent datum is a family of objects $x_i\in F(U_i)$ with [isomorphisms](c:isomorphism) $\varphi_{ij}:p_1^*x_i\to p_2^*x_j$ over the overlaps $U_i\times_U U_j$ that satisfy $\varphi_{ik}=\varphi_{jk}\circ\varphi_{ij}$ over triple overlaps. The category of descent data has these data as objects and the families of morphisms $x_i\to y_i$ that commute with the $\varphi_{ij}$ as morphisms; it is the 2-categorical [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of the cosimplicial diagram of the categories $F(U_i)$, $F(U_i\times_U U_j)$, and so on.
examples: For an open cover $\{U_i\}$ of a space $X$ and $F(U)$ the category of [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) on $U$, a descent datum is a family of bundles $E_i$ on $U_i$ with gluing isomorphisms on the overlaps.

For a [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) ring map $A\to B$, a descent datum is a $B$-module $N$ with an isomorphism $N\otimes_A B\cong B\otimes_A N$ that obeys the cocycle condition, and the category of such data is equivalent to $A$-modules.
For the trivial cover $\{U\to U\}$, a descent datum is just one object of $F(U)$, because the cocycle condition forces the gluing isomorphism to be the identity.
Non-example: local objects $x_i$ with isomorphisms $\varphi_{ij}$ that fail the cocycle condition on some triple overlap are not descent data, and they do not glue to a global object.

reminder: The Cauchy principal value omits a small symmetric interval around a singularity and takes the limit as it shrinks.
definition: Let $c\in(a,b)$ and let $f$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a,c-\varepsilon]$ and on $[c+\varepsilon,b]$ for every small $\varepsilon>0$. The Cauchy principal value of $f$ is $\mathrm{p.v.}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\Big(\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}f+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^b f\Big)$, when this [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) exists.
examples: $\mathrm{p.v.}\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dx}{x}=0$, because the two pieces of $1/x$ cancel for every $\varepsilon$, although $\int_{-1}^{1}dx/x$ does not exist as an [improper integral](c:improper-integral).
The principal value of $1/x$ defines a [distribution](c:distribution) by $\varphi\mapsto\mathrm{p.v.}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ for test functions $\varphi$.
If the [improper integral](c:improper-integral) of $f$ at $c$ converges, the principal value exists and has the same value.
Non-example: $\int_{-1}^{1}dx/x^2$ has no finite principal value, because both one-sided pieces tend to $+\infty$ and their sum is $2/\varepsilon-2$.

steps: Take $f$ whose [improper integral](c:improper-integral) at $c$ converges, so both one-sided pieces have limits $L_1$ and $L_2$.
Use the same $\varepsilon$ on both sides, which is one special way to approach $c$.
Then the symmetric sum tends to $L_1+L_2$, which is the improper integral.
So the principal value exists and equals the improper integral, and the converse fails for $1/x$.
links.why: It shows that the principal value extends the ordinary improper integral and still gives a value when the improper integral does not exist.

reminder: Cellular homology is the homology of a chain complex with one free generator for each cell of a CW complex.
definition: Let $X$ be a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with skeleta $X^n$. The cellular [chain complex](c:chain-complex) has $C_n=H_n(X^n,X^{n-1})$, a free abelian group with one generator for each $n$-cell, and its differential is the composite $H_n(X^n,X^{n-1})\to H_{n-1}(X^{n-1})\to H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2})$, whose entries are [degrees](c:degree-of-a-continuous-function) of maps between spheres. The cellular homology of $X$ is the [homology](c:homology) of this complex, and it is [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) to the singular homology of $X$.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ with one $0$-cell and one $n$-cell has $C_0=C_n=\mathbb Z$ and zero differentials, so $H_0=H_n=\mathbb Z$ and all other groups vanish.
The [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space) $\mathbb{CP}^n$ has one cell in each dimension $0,2,\dots,2n$, so all differentials vanish and $H_{2k}=\mathbb Z$ for $0\le k\le n$.
The real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ has one cell in each dimension $0,1,2$ with $d_1=0$ and $d_2=2$, so $H_1=\mathbb Z/2$ and $H_2=0$.
Non-example: the Hawaiian earring is not a CW complex, so it has no cellular chain complex.

reminder: A central character of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ is an [algebra homomorphism](c:alg-hom) from the [center](c:center) of $U(\mathfrak g)$ to $\mathbb C$.
definition: Let $U(\mathfrak g)$ be the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ over $\mathbb C$, and let $Z(\mathfrak g)$ be its [center](c:center). A central character is an [algebra homomorphism](c:alg-hom) $\chi:Z(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb C$. A [module](c:module) $M$ has central character $\chi$ when every $z\in Z(\mathfrak g)$ acts on $M$ as the scalar $\chi(z)$.
examples: For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$ the [Casimir element](c:casimir-operator) $C=ef+fe+\tfrac12h^2$ generates $Z(\mathfrak g)$, and it acts on the irreducible module of highest weight $n$ as the scalar $n(n+2)/2$.
A [Verma module](c:verma-module) $M(\lambda)$ has a central character $\chi_\lambda$, because $Z(\mathfrak g)$ acts by a scalar on the highest weight vector that generates $M(\lambda)$.
For a semisimple $\mathfrak g$, $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ exactly when $\mu$ lies in the dot-orbit of $\lambda$ under the [Weyl group](c:weyl-group) (Harish-Chandra).
Non-example: for a central character $\chi$ the map $2\chi$ is linear but sends $1$ to $2$, so it is not an algebra homomorphism.

reminder: A chain-complete poset is a partially ordered set in which every chain has a least upper bound.
definition: A [partially ordered](c:partial-order) set $(P,\le)$ is chain-complete when every [totally ordered](c:total-order) subset $C\subseteq P$ has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) in $P$. The empty chain is a chain, so $P$ then has a least element; some authors ask this only for nonempty chains and add a least element as a separate assumption.
examples: Every [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice) is chain-complete, for example the power set of a set ordered by inclusion, where the union of a chain is its least upper bound.
The closed interval $[0,1]$ with its usual order is chain-complete, because every subset has a least upper bound.
Every [dcpo](c:dcpo) with a least element is chain-complete, because every chain is directed.
Non-example: $\mathbb N$ with its usual order is not chain-complete, because the chain $\mathbb N$ has no upper bound.

steps: Take a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice) $L$, where every subset has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound).
A chain in $L$ is a subset of $L$, so it has a least upper bound in $L$.
So $L$ is chain-complete, and the converse fails: two incomparable elements above a least element form a chain-complete poset that is not a lattice.
links.why: It shows that chain-completeness asks only for least upper bounds of chains, so fixed point arguments for lattices carry over to many more posets.

steps: Take a [dcpo](c:dcpo) $D$ with a least element, so every directed subset has a supremum.
A nonempty chain in $D$ is directed, so it has a supremum in $D$.
The empty chain has the least element as its supremum, so $D$ is chain-complete.
links.why: It lets a learner use results about chain-complete posets, such as the Bourbaki-Witt theorem, on the posets of domain theory.

reminder: A chain homotopy between chain maps $f,g$ is a degree-one map $h$ with $f-g=dh+hd$.
definition: Let $f,g:C\to D$ be [chain maps](c:chain-map) of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex). A chain homotopy from $f$ to $g$ is a family of [homomorphisms](c:homomorphism) $h_n:C_n\to D_{n+1}$ with $f_n-g_n=d_{n+1}h_n+h_{n-1}d_n$ for all $n$. Equivalently, it is a chain map $C\otimes I\to D$ out of the product with the standard [interval object](c:interval-object-in-chain-complexes) that restricts to $f$ and $g$ at the two ends.
examples: If $C$ is a [contractible chain complex](c:contractible-chain-complex), the identity of $C$ is chain homotopic to $0$ through a contracting homotopy $h$.
For homotopic maps $f\simeq g$ of spaces, the prism operator is a chain homotopy between the induced maps on singular chains.
Chain homotopic maps induce the same map on [homology](c:homology): if $f-g=dh+hd$ and $dz=0$, then $f(z)-g(z)=d\,h(z)$ is a boundary.
Non-example: on the complex with $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$ only, the maps $\mathrm{id}$ and $0$ are not chain homotopic, because $D_1=0$ forces $h=0$ and $\mathrm{id}\ne0$.

steps: A [homotopy](c:homotopy) between maps $f$ and $g$ is a map out of the product with an interval that restricts to $f$ and $g$ at the ends.
Work with [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) and take the standard chain complex $I$ of the interval as the interval object.
A map $C\otimes I\to D$ that restricts to $f$ and $g$ unpacks to degree-one maps $h_n$ with $f-g=dh+hd$.
links.why: It explains the formula $dh+hd$ as the ordinary notion of homotopy, written out inside chain complexes.

reminder: A characteristic class assigns to each bundle a cohomology class of its base, compatible with pullback.
definition: A characteristic class $c$ of [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) or [principal bundles](c:principal-bundle) with values in [cohomology](c:cohomology) assigns to each bundle $E\to X$ a class $c(E)\in H^*(X)$. It is natural: for every map $f:Y\to X$ we have $c(f^*E)=f^*c(E)$, where $f^*E$ is the [pullback](c:pullback) bundle.
examples: The [Stiefel-Whitney classes](c:stiefel-whitney-class) $w_i(E)\in H^i(X;\mathbb Z/2)$ of real vector bundles.
The [Chern classes](c:chern-class) $c_i(E)\in H^{2i}(X;\mathbb Z)$ of complex vector bundles, and the [Euler class](c:euler-class) of an oriented bundle.
On paracompact bases, the characteristic classes of rank $n$ real bundles correspond to the elements of $H^*(BO(n))$, through the universal bundle over the [classifying space](c:classifying-space).
Non-example: giving every bundle over $S^2$ the generator of $H^2(S^2)$ is not natural, because pulling back along a constant map of $S^2$ gives the generator on one side and $0$ on the other.

steps: Take the assignment $E\mapsto w_i(E)\in H^i(X;\mathbb Z/2)$ on real vector bundles.
Naturality is one of the axioms: $w_i(f^*E)=f^*w_i(E)$ for every map $f$.
So each [Stiefel-Whitney class](c:stiefel-whitney-class) is a characteristic class with $\mathbb Z/2$ coefficients.
links.why: It shows that naturality, not the particular construction, is what makes a class characteristic.

steps: Take the assignment $E\mapsto c_i(E)\in H^{2i}(X;\mathbb Z)$ on complex vector bundles.
Naturality is one of the axioms: $c_i(f^*E)=f^*c_i(E)$ for every map $f$.
So each [Chern class](c:chern-class) is a characteristic class with integer coefficients.
links.why: It gives a second family of examples, and shows that the same naturality rule covers real and complex bundles.

reminder: A charge conjugation matrix is the matrix of an invariant bilinear form on spinors.
definition: Let $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_d$ be gamma matrices, the matrices of the generators of a [Clifford algebra](c:clifford-algebra), acting on a [spinor](c:spinor) space $S$. A charge conjugation matrix is an invertible [matrix](c:matrix) $C$ with $C\gamma_\mu C^{-1}=\varepsilon\,\gamma_\mu^{T}$ for all $\mu$ and one fixed sign $\varepsilon=\pm1$. Then $B(\psi,\chi)=\psi^TC\chi$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on $S$ that is invariant under the [spin representation](c:spin-representation).
examples: For $d=3$ with the Pauli matrices $\sigma_i$ as gamma matrices, $C=i\sigma_2$ works with $\varepsilon=-1$, and $B$ is the antisymmetric invariant form $\psi_1\chi_2-\psi_2\chi_1$ on $\mathbb C^2$.
In four-dimensional Minkowski space, a common convention in the Dirac representation is $C=i\gamma^2\gamma^0$.
Non-example: the identity matrix is not a charge conjugation matrix for the Pauli matrices, because $\sigma_2^T=-\sigma_2$ but $\sigma_1^T=\sigma_1$, so no single sign $\varepsilon$ works.

steps: Choose a basis of the spinor space $S$ and write a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$ on $S$ by its matrix $C$, so $B(\psi,\chi)=\psi^TC\chi$.
Require $B$ to be invariant under the [spin representation](c:spin-representation).
Invariance follows from the relation $C\gamma_\mu C^{-1}=\varepsilon\gamma_\mu^T$ between $C$ and the gamma matrices.
links.why: It shows that the charge conjugation matrix is only the matrix of a bilinear form, with one extra symmetry condition.

reminder: The Chern connection of a Hermitian holomorphic bundle is the unique connection that preserves the metric and the holomorphic structure.
definition: Let $E$ be a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) with a Hermitian metric $h$. The Chern connection is the unique [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $\nabla$ on $E$ that preserves $h$ and whose $(0,1)$-part is the $\bar\partial$-operator of $E$, so $\nabla^{0,1}=\bar\partial_E$.
examples: In a local holomorphic frame $e$ of a line bundle with $h=|e|^2$, the connection form is $\partial\log h$, so $\nabla e=\partial\log h\otimes e$.
On a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold), the Chern connection of the holomorphic tangent bundle with the Kähler metric agrees with the [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection).
For the trivial line bundle with $h=1$, the Chern connection is the ordinary derivative $d$.
Non-example: on the trivial line bundle with a non-constant metric $h$, the flat connection $d$ has $(0,1)$-part $\bar\partial$ but does not preserve $h$, so it is not the Chern connection.

steps:
Start with a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $
abla$ on the holomorphic bundle $E$ and split it as $
abla=
abla^{1,0}+
abla^{0,1}$.
Require $\nabla^{0,1}=\bar\partial_E$, so that $\nabla$ respects the holomorphic structure.
Require $\nabla$ to preserve the Hermitian metric $h$.
These two conditions fix $\nabla$ uniquely, and the result is the Chern connection.
links.why: It shows that the Chern connection is an ordinary connection singled out by two compatibility conditions.

reminder: The Christoffel symbols are the coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ of an affine connection in local coordinates.
definition: Let $\nabla$ be an [affine connection](c:affine-connection) on a [manifold](c:manifold) with local coordinates $x^1,\dots,x^n$. The Christoffel symbols are the functions $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ defined by $\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k$. For the [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection) of a metric $g$ they are $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_l g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$.
examples: In Cartesian coordinates on $\mathbb R^2$ with the flat metric, all $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ are $0$.
In polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-r$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}=1/r$, and all others are $0$.
On the round unit sphere with coordinates $(\theta,\phi)$, the nonzero symbols are $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\Gamma^\phi_{\phi\theta}=\cot\theta$.
Non-example: the symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ are not the components of a tensor, because they vanish in Cartesian coordinates on $\mathbb R^2$ but not in polar coordinates.

steps: Take the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) with the local frame $\partial_1,\dots,\partial_n$ given by the coordinates.
A [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on it has a local matrix of $1$-forms $\omega^k{}_j$ with $\nabla\partial_j=\sum_k\omega^k{}_j\,\partial_k$.
Expand each $1$-form in the coordinate basis as $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k_{ij}\,dx^i$.
The coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols.
links.why: It shows that Christoffel symbols are the local connection coefficients of the tangent bundle in a coordinate frame.

reminder: The chromatic tower of a spectrum $X$ is the tower of its localizations $L_nX$ at Morava E-theory, from height $n$ down to $0$.
definition: Fix a [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ and let $X$ be a [p-local spectrum](c:p-local-spectrum). Let $L_nX$ be the [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) of $X$ at [Morava E-theory](c:morava-e-theory) $E_n$, which has the same Bousfield class as the Johnson-Wilson theory $E(n)$. The chromatic tower is the diagram $\cdots\to L_nX\to L_{n-1}X\to\cdots\to L_1X\to L_0X$ of localizations under $X$.
examples: The bottom stage $L_0X$ is the rationalization of $X$, and the fiber of $L_nX\to L_{n-1}X$ is the [monochromatic layer](c:monochromatic-layer) $M_nX$.
By the chromatic convergence theorem, for a finite $p$-local spectrum such as the $p$-local sphere $S_{(p)}$ the [homotopy limit](c:homotopy-limit) of the tower is $S_{(p)}$ itself.
Non-example: the Postnikov tower of $X$ is also a tower under $X$, but its stages truncate homotopy groups by degree and are not localizations by chromatic height.

reminder: The circle group is the group of complex numbers of modulus one under multiplication.
definition: The circle group $\mathbb T=U(1)$ is the set $\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with complex multiplication, a [group](c:group) whose topology is that of the [circle](c:circle). The map $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of topological groups from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb T$, so $\mathbb T$ is also a [quotient group](c:quotient-group) of the real line by the integers.
examples: Since $e^{i\theta}e^{i\varphi}=e^{i(\theta+\varphi)}$, multiplying two points of $\mathbb T$ adds their angles.
The $n$th [roots of unity](c:roots-of-unity) form a finite subgroup of $\mathbb T$ of order $n$.
Rotation of the plane by the angle $\theta$ corresponds to $e^{i\theta}$, so $\mathbb T$ is isomorphic to the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group) $SO(2)$.
Non-example: the multiplicative group $\mathbb C^\times$ is not the circle group, because it contains numbers of modulus different from $1$; $\mathbb T$ is only its subgroup of modulus-one elements.

steps: The [unitary group](c:unitary-group) $U(n)$ consists of the complex $n\times n$ matrices $A$ with $A^*A=I$.
Take $n=1$: a $1\times1$ matrix is a complex number $z$, and the condition reads $\bar zz=1$.
This says $|z|=1$, and matrix multiplication is complex multiplication.
So $U(1)$ is the circle group $\mathbb T$.
links.why: It places the circle group as the smallest unitary group, which explains why it appears as a phase group in physics.

steps: Give $\mathbb T$ the structure of a smooth manifold as the unit circle in $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$.
Multiplication $(z,w)\mapsto zw$ and inversion $z\mapsto\bar z$ are polynomial in the real coordinates, so they are smooth.
So $\mathbb T$ is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) of dimension one.
links.why: It shows that the circle group is the simplest compact connected Lie group, so Lie theory applies to it.

reminder: The circumcircle of a triangle is the unique circle that passes through all three vertices.
definition: For a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ whose vertices are not collinear, the circumcircle is the [circle](c:circle) through its three [vertices](c:vertex). Its centre is the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter), the common point of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides, and its radius is the circumradius $R$.
examples: In a right triangle the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so $R$ is half the hypotenuse.
An equilateral triangle with side $a$ has circumradius $R=a/\sqrt3$.
A triangle has a circumcircle exactly when its vertices are not collinear; polygons that have a circumcircle are [cyclic polygons](c:cyclic-polygon).
Non-example: the [incircle](c:incircle) touches the three sides from inside and does not pass through the vertices, so it is not the circumcircle.

steps: Take a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ with non-collinear vertices and look for a [circle](c:circle) that passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.
Its centre is equidistant from $A$ and $B$, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and the same holds for $BC$.
These two bisectors are not parallel, so they meet in exactly one point $O$.
The circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ is the circumcircle.
links.why: It shows that the extra condition of passing through three given points picks out exactly one circle.

reminder: The classifying topos of a geometric theory $T$ represents models of $T$: geometric morphisms $E\to\mathcal S[T]$ are $T$-models in $E$.
definition: Let $T$ be a [geometric theory](c:geometric-theory). A classifying topos of $T$ is a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) $\mathcal S[T]$ with a universal model $U$ of $T$ in it, such that for every Grothendieck topos $E$ the assignment $f\mapsto f^*U$ is an equivalence of categories from the [geometric morphisms](c:geometric-morphism) $E\to\mathcal S[T]$ to the models of $T$ in $E$.
examples: The [classifying topos for the theory of objects](c:classifying-topos-for-the-theory-of-objects) has geometric morphisms from $E$ that correspond to the objects of $E$.
For a discrete group $G$, the topos $BG$ of $G$-sets classifies $G$-torsors: a geometric morphism $E\to BG$ is a $G$-torsor in $E$.
Every geometric theory has a classifying topos, built as the topos of sheaves on the syntactic site of the theory.
Non-example: the topos $\mathbf{Set}$ is not a classifying topos for the theory of objects, because a geometric morphism $E\to\mathbf{Set}$ is unique up to isomorphism while objects of $E$ are not.

steps: Take the [geometric theory](c:geometric-theory) of objects, with one sort, no function symbols and no axioms.
A model of this theory in a topos $E$ is just an object of $E$.
A classifying topos for it has geometric morphisms from $E$ that correspond to objects of $E$.
So the classifying topos for the theory of objects is the case where $T$ is this simplest theory.
links.why: It gives a concrete first instance: the classifying topos of the simplest theory, whose models are just objects.

reminder: A cleavage chooses a cartesian lift for each base morphism $f:b'\to b$ and each object over $b$.
definition: Let $p:E\to B$ be a [functor](c:functor). A cleavage of $p$ is a choice, for every morphism $f:b'\to b$ of $B$ and every object $e$ of $E$ over $b$, of a [cartesian morphism](c:cartesian-morphism) $f^*e\to e$ over $f$. A functor with a cleavage is a [Grothendieck fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration), and the cleavage is split when $\mathrm{id}^*e=e$ and $(gf)^*=f^*g^*$ hold strictly.
examples: For a category $C$ with [pullbacks](c:pullback), the codomain functor $C^{\to}\to C$ has a cleavage: for $f:b'\to b$ and an arrow $e\to b$, choose a pullback square.
For a functor $F:C^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$, the Grothendieck construction gives a fibration over $C$ with a split cleavage given by $f^*x=F(f)(x)$.
With the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice), every Grothendieck fibration has a cleavage, because one can pick a cartesian lift for each pair $(f,e)$.
Non-example: the inclusion of a one-object category $\{e\}$ as the object $1$ of the category $0\to1$ has no cleavage, since no object lies over $0$ to receive a lift of $0\to1$.

reminder: The Clifford group on $n$ qubits is the normalizer of the Pauli group in the unitary group $U(2^n)$.
definition: Let $P_n$ be the [Pauli group](c:pauli-group) on $n$ [qubits](c:qbit), generated by the $n$-fold tensor products of Pauli matrices and phases. The Clifford group is the [normalizer](c:normalizer) $\{U\in U(2^n):UP_nU^{-1}=P_n\}$ of $P_n$ in the [unitary group](c:unitary-group) $U(2^n)$. Its elements are the unitaries, or [quantum gates](c:quantum-gate), that map Pauli operators to Pauli operators by conjugation.
examples: The Hadamard gate $H$, the phase gate $S=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)$ and the CNOT gate lie in the Clifford group, and together they generate it up to phases.
Every Pauli matrix lies in the Clifford group, because conjugating a Pauli matrix by a Pauli matrix gives the same matrix up to a sign.
Circuits of Clifford gates with stabilizer inputs and Pauli measurements can be simulated in polynomial time on a classical computer (Gottesman-Knill).
Non-example: the $T$ gate $\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})$ is not Clifford, because $TXT^{-1}=(X+Y)/\sqrt2$ is not a Pauli matrix up to a phase.

steps: Take the group $G=U(2^n)$ of [unitary operators](c:unitary-operator) on $n$ qubits and its subgroup $H=P_n$.
The [normalizer](c:normalizer) $N_G(H)$ consists of the $g\in G$ with $gHg^{-1}=H$.
For $H=P_n$ these are the unitaries that conjugate Pauli operators to Pauli operators.
So the Clifford group is the normalizer $N_{U(2^n)}(P_n)$.
links.why: It lets a learner reuse normalizer facts, for example that the Clifford group acts on the Pauli group by conjugation.

reminder: An abstract clone is a family of sets of $n$-ary operations with projections and an associative, unital composition.
definition: An abstract clone $C$ is a family of sets $C(n)$ for $n\ge0$, with projections $\pi^n_i\in C(n)$ for $1\le i\le n$ and a composition $C(m)\times C(n)^m\to C(n)$, written $(f,g_1,\dots,g_m)\mapsto f(g_1,\dots,g_m)$. Composition is associative and the projections are units: $\pi^m_i(g_1,\dots,g_m)=g_i$ and $f(\pi^n_1,\dots,\pi^n_n)=f$. It describes a single-sorted [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory) without a choice of presentation.
examples: For a set $A$, the clone of all [operations](c:operation) has $C(n)=A^{A^n}$, with the usual projections and composition of functions.
For the theory of groups, $C(n)$ is the set of group words in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and composition is substitution.
Non-example: the constant operations $A^n\to A$ on a set with at least two elements are closed under composition but contain no projection, so they do not form a clone.

steps: Take a [cartesian multicategory](c:cartesian-multicategory) with exactly one object $*$.
Its multimorphisms with $n$ inputs $*,\dots,*\to*$ form a set $C(n)$.
The cartesian structure gives the projections $\pi^n_i$, and composition of multimorphisms gives the substitution.
The associativity and unit laws of the multicategory are the clone axioms.
links.why: It shows that a clone is a one-object cartesian multicategory, so multicategory tools apply to algebraic theories.

reminder: A closed cofibration is a Hurewicz cofibration whose image is a closed subspace.
definition: A map $i:A\to X$ of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is a closed cofibration when it is a [Hurewicz cofibration](c:hurewicz-cofibration), that is, it has the homotopy extension property, and it is a [closed embedding](c:is-closed-embedding). Equivalently, $A$ is closed in $X$ and $(X,A)$ is a neighborhood deformation retract pair.
examples: The inclusion $S^{n-1}\to D^n$ of the boundary sphere is a closed cofibration.
The inclusion of a subcomplex into a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is a closed cofibration.
The inclusion of a closed smooth submanifold into a smooth manifold is a closed cofibration.

Non-example: the inclusion of $\{0\}$ into $X=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}\subset\mathbb R$ is a closed embedding but not a cofibration, because each point $1/n$ near $0$ would need a path in $X$ to $0$ and $X$ has no nonconstant paths.

steps: Take a [Hurewicz cofibration](c:hurewicz-cofibration) $i:A\to X$, a map with the homotopy extension property.
Add one condition: the image $i(A)$ is closed in $X$.
Such a map is a closed cofibration, and when $X$ is Hausdorff every Hurewicz cofibration already satisfies the condition.
links.why: It shows that closedness is the only extra condition, and that it comes for free in the Hausdorff case.

steps: Give the category of topological spaces the Strøm model structure, whose weak equivalences are the homotopy equivalences.
In this model structure the fibrations are the Hurewicz fibrations and the cofibrations are the closed Hurewicz cofibrations.
So a closed cofibration is a cofibration in the sense of model categories.
links.why: It shows where closed cofibrations sit inside the general model-categorical notion of cofibration.

reminder: A closed subgroup of a topological group is a subgroup that is a closed subset.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group). A closed subgroup of $G$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H\le G$ that is a [closed set](c:closed-set) in the topology of $G$. The closure $\bar H$ of any subgroup $H$ is a closed subgroup, and $H$ is closed exactly when $H=\bar H$.
examples: $\mathbb Z$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathbb R$.
$SL_n(\mathbb R)$ is a closed subgroup of $GL_n(\mathbb R)$, because it is the zero set of the continuous function $\det-1$.
Every closed subgroup of a Lie group is a Lie subgroup (Cartan's closed subgroup theorem).
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb R$ that is not closed, because its closure is all of $\mathbb R$.

steps: Take a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$, so $H$ is closed under products and inverses.
Add the topological condition that $H$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set) in $G$.
Then $H$ is a closed subgroup, and it is itself a topological group in the subspace topology.
links.why: It shows that closedness is a topological condition added to the algebraic one, and that it makes the quotient $G/H$ well behaved.

reminder: An $n$-cochain with coefficients in $A$ is a homomorphism from the group of $n$-chains to $A$.
definition: Let $C_*$ be a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) and $A$ an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). An $n$-cochain of $C_*$ with coefficients in $A$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\varphi:C_n\to A$, so it evaluates each $n$-[chain](c:chain). The coboundary $\delta\varphi=\varphi\circ\partial_{n+1}$, up to a sign, is an $(n+1)$-cochain, and the cochains form a cochain complex.
examples: On the singular chains of a space $X$, an $n$-cochain assigns an element of $A$ to each singular $n$-simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ and extends linearly.
A [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $n$ on a manifold gives the real cochain $\sigma\mapsto\int_\sigma\omega$ on smooth singular simplices.
On a CW complex, a cellular $n$-cochain assigns a value to each $n$-cell.
Non-example: a singular simplex $\sigma$, or a sum of simplices, is an $n$-chain and not an $n$-cochain, because a cochain is a function on chains.

reminder: A cocone under a diagram is an object with a morphism from each vertex such that all triangles commute.
definition: Let $D:J\to C$ be a [diagram](c:diagram) in a [category](c:category). A cocone under $D$ is an object $N$ of $C$ with morphisms $\psi_j:D(j)\to N$ for all objects $j$ of $J$ such that $\psi_{j'}\circ D(u)=\psi_j$ for every morphism $u:j\to j'$ of $J$. A [colimit](c:colimit) of $D$ is a cocone that is initial among all cocones under $D$.
examples: For a pair of objects $X,Y$ as a discrete diagram, a cocone is an object $N$ with maps $X\to N$ and $Y\to N$, and the [coproduct](c:coproduct) is the universal one.
For a span $B\leftarrow A\to C$, a cocone is a commutative square, and the [pushout](c:pushout) is the universal one.
For a chain of inclusions of sets $X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots$, the union with its inclusion maps is the universal cocone.
Non-example: for a parallel pair $f,g:A\rightrightarrows B$, a map $\psi_B:B\to N$ with $\psi_Bf\ne\psi_Bg$ gives no cocone, because both triangles must commute with the same $\psi_A$.

steps: Take a [colimit](c:colimit) $L$ of the diagram $D$, which comes with maps $\lambda_j:D(j)\to L$.
These maps satisfy $\lambda_{j'}\circ D(u)=\lambda_j$ for every morphism $u:j\to j'$.
So $(L,\lambda)$ is a cocone under $D$.
It is the initial cocone, so every other cocone factors uniquely through it.
links.why: It shows that a colimit is a cocone with one extra property, the universal one.

reminder: The codimension of a subspace is the dimension of the whole space minus the dimension of the subspace.
definition: Let $W$ be a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$. The codimension of $W$ in $V$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) of the quotient space $V/W$, and it equals $\dim V-\dim W$ when $\dim V$ is finite. The same number $d-k$ is the codimension of a $k$-dimensional [submanifold](c:submanifold) of a $d$-dimensional [manifold](c:manifold).
examples: A plane through the origin in $\mathbb R^3$ has codimension $1$, and a line through the origin has codimension $2$.
The kernel of a nonzero linear functional on $V$ is a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane), a subspace of codimension $1$.
The sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ is a submanifold of codimension $1$.
Non-example: the $x$-axis in $\mathbb R^3$ does not have codimension $1$, because $3-1=2$.

reminder: The cofiber of a morphism $f:A\to B$ is the pushout of $f$ along the map from $A$ to the terminal object.
definition: Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in a [category](c:category) with a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) $1$. The cofiber of $f$ is the [pushout](c:pushout) $B\sqcup_A1$ of the span $1\leftarrow A\xrightarrow{f}B$. For a [cofibration](c:cofibration) such as the inclusion of a subcomplex, it is the quotient $B/A$, which is homotopy equivalent to the [mapping cone](c:mapping-cone) of $f$.
examples: For the inclusion $S^{n-1}\to D^n$, the cofiber is $D^n/S^{n-1}\cong S^n$.
In abelian groups, the cofiber of $f:A\to B$ is the quotient $B/f(A)$, which is the cokernel of $f$.
The homotopy cofiber of the degree $2$ map $S^1\to S^1$ is the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$.
Non-example: the pullback $A\times_B1$ of a pointed map $f$ along the basepoint is its fiber, the dual construction, and not its cofiber.

steps: Take $f:A\to B$ and the unique morphism $t:A\to1$ to the [terminal object](c:terminal-object).
Form the [pushout](c:pushout) of the span $1\xleftarrow{t}A\xrightarrow{f}B$.
The object $B\sqcup_A1$ is the cofiber of $f$.
links.why: It shows that the cofiber is not a new construction: it is the pushout of one special span.

reminder: A cofibration is a morphism with the left lifting property against all acyclic fibrations.
definition: In a [model category](c:model-category), a cofibration is a morphism that has the [left lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against every [acyclic fibration](c:acyclic-fibration). It is dual to a [fibration](c:fibration), which has the right lifting property against every acyclic cofibration.
examples: In the Kan-Quillen model structure on [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set), the cofibrations are the monomorphisms, that is, the injective maps.
In the Quillen model structure on topological spaces, the inclusion of a subcomplex of a [CW complex](c:cw-complex), such as $S^{n-1}\to D^n$, is a cofibration.
The boundary inclusions $\partial\Delta^n\to\Delta^n$ are cofibrations of simplicial sets, and they generate all cofibrations.
Non-example: the surjection $\Delta^1\to\Delta^0$ of simplicial sets is not a cofibration, because it is not injective.

steps: Give the category of topological spaces the Strøm model structure, whose weak equivalences are the homotopy equivalences.
In this model structure the fibrations are the Hurewicz fibrations and the cofibrations are the closed Hurewicz cofibrations.
So every [closed cofibration](c:closed-cofibration) $i:A\to X$ is a cofibration of this model category.
links.why: It shows where the topological notion of a closed cofibration sits inside the general notion of a cofibration.

reminder: The cofinality of an ordered set is the least size of a subset that is cofinal in it.
definition: A subset $C$ of a [partially ordered](c:partial-order) set $P$ is [cofinal](c:cofinal) if every $p\in P$ lies below some element of $C$. The cofinality $\operatorname{cf}(P)$ is the least [cardinality](c:cardinal-number) of a cofinal subset of $P$. For a limit [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ this is the least cardinal $\kappa$ such that some map $\kappa\to\alpha$ has cofinal image.
examples: $\operatorname{cf}(\omega\cdot2)=\aleph_0$, because $\{\omega+n:n<\omega\}$ is cofinal in $\omega\cdot2=\omega+\omega$.
$\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega)=\aleph_0$, because $\{\aleph_n:n<\omega\}$ is cofinal in $\aleph_\omega$, while $\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_1)=\aleph_1$.
The real line $\mathbb R$ with its usual order has cofinality $\aleph_0$, because $\mathbb N$ is cofinal in it.
Non-example: $\omega_1$ does not have cofinality $\aleph_0$, because every countable subset of $\omega_1$ is bounded below $\omega_1$, so no countable subset is cofinal.

reminder: An object $S$ is a cogenerator when maps into $S$ separate every pair of different parallel morphisms.
definition: An object $S$ of a [category](c:category) $C$ is a cogenerator if the [hom functor](c:hom-functor) $C(-,S):C^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is [faithful](c:faithful). Equivalently, for all $g_1\ne g_2:X\to Y$ there is a morphism $\theta:Y\to S$ with $\theta g_1\ne\theta g_2$.
examples: In $\mathbf{Set}$ every two-element set is a cogenerator: two different functions differ at some point $x$, and a map from the target to $\{0,1\}$ can separate their two values at $x$.
In abelian groups, $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is a cogenerator.
In vector spaces over a field $k$, the field $k$ itself is a cogenerator.
Non-example: in abelian groups $\mathbb Z$ is not a cogenerator, because $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb Z)=0$ cannot tell the identity of $\mathbb Z/2$ from the zero map.

reminder: The cohomology ring of a space $X$ is the graded ring $\bigoplus_nH^n(X)$ with the cup product.
definition: Let $E$ be a [multiplicative cohomology theory](c:multiplicative-cohomology-theory), such as ordinary cohomology with coefficients in a [ring](c:ring) $R$, and let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space). The cohomology ring is the [graded abelian group](c:graded-abelian-group) $E^*(X)=\bigoplus_nE^n(X)$ with the product induced by the [cup product](c:cup-product), which makes it a [graded ring](c:graded-ring). For ordinary cohomology with commutative coefficients it is graded commutative: $ab=(-1)^{|a||b|}ba$.
examples: $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{n+1})$ with $|x|=2$.
$H^*(S^n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2)$ with $|x|=n$.
$H^*(T^2;\mathbb Z)$ is the exterior algebra on two classes $a,b$ of degree $1$, with $ab=-ba$ and $a^2=b^2=0$.
Non-example: the homology groups $H_*(X)$ of a general space form a graded abelian group but carry no natural cup product, so they do not form a cohomology ring.

steps: Take the [graded abelian group](c:graded-abelian-group) $H^*(X;R)=\bigoplus_nH^n(X;R)$.
Define the product of $a\in H^p$ and $b\in H^q$ as the [cup product](c:cup-product) $a\smile b\in H^{p+q}$.
The cup product is associative and bilinear with a unit $1\in H^0$, so $H^*(X;R)$ is a [graded ring](c:graded-ring).
A map $f:X\to Y$ induces a ring homomorphism $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$.
links.why: It shows that a cohomology ring is an ordinary graded ring with one extra property: it is natural in the space.

reminder: The cohomotopy set $\pi^n(X)$ is the set of homotopy classes of maps from $X$ to the sphere $S^n$.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and $n\ge0$, the cohomotopy set is $\pi^n(X)=[X,S^n]$, the set of [homotopy](c:homotopy) classes of continuous maps from $X$ to the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$. It is a contravariant functor of $X$, and it is an abelian group when $X$ is a suspension or has dimension at most $2n-2$.
examples: For a CW complex $X$ of dimension at most $n$, $\pi^n(X)\cong H^n(X;\mathbb Z)$ (Hopf).
$\pi^n(S^n)\cong\mathbb Z$, where a class is sent to the [degree](c:degree-of-a-continuous-function) of a representing map.
For a closed manifold $M$, the set $\pi^n(M)$ is in bijection with framed codimension-$n$ submanifolds of $M$ up to framed cobordism (Pontryagin).
Non-example: the set $[S^n,X]$ of maps from the sphere into $X$ is the homotopy set $\pi_n(X)$, not the cohomotopy set, because cohomotopy takes maps into the sphere.

reminder: The cokernel of a morphism $f:A\to B$ is the universal map out of $B$ that sends $f$ to zero.
definition: In a [category](c:category) with a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) $1$, the cokernel of $f:A\to B$ is the [pushout](c:pushout) $B\sqcup_A1$. When $1$ is also initial, it is a map $q:B\to C$ with $qf=0$ such that every $g:B\to D$ with $gf=0$ factors uniquely through $q$.
examples: In [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) and in [vector spaces](c:vector-space), $\operatorname{coker}f=B/\operatorname{im}f$.
For the map $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $x\mapsto2x$, the cokernel is $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.
For a matrix $M:k^n\to k^m$, the cokernel is $k^m/\operatorname{col}(M)$, of dimension $m-\operatorname{rank}M$.
Non-example: the image $2\mathbb Z$ of $x\mapsto2x$ is a subobject of the target and not a quotient, so it is not the cokernel.

steps: Start with the span $1\leftarrow A\xrightarrow{f}B$ in a category with a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) $1$.
Its [pushout](c:pushout) is an object $C$ with maps $q:B\to C$ and $1\to C$.
When $1$ is a zero object, the square gives $qf=0$, and the universal property gives the factorization of every $g$ with $gf=0$.
So the cokernel is the pushout of this special span.
links.why: It shows that the cokernel is a pushout in which one leg of the span goes to the terminal object.

reminder: A combinatorial model category is a cofibrantly generated model category whose underlying category is locally presentable.
definition: A [model category](c:model-category) $M$ is combinatorial if its underlying category is [locally presentable](c:locally-presentable-category) and $M$ is [cofibrantly generated](c:cofibrantly-generated-model-category): the cofibrations and the acyclic cofibrations are generated by small sets $I$ and $J$ of morphisms. The small object argument then builds the factorizations from $I$ and $J$.
examples: The Kan-Quillen model structure on [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set) is combinatorial.
The projective model structure on unbounded chain complexes of modules over a ring is combinatorial.
For a small category $C$ and a combinatorial model category $M$, the projective model structure on the functors $C\to M$ exists and is combinatorial.
Non-example: the Quillen model structure on topological spaces is cofibrantly generated but not combinatorial, because the category of topological spaces is not locally presentable.

steps: Take a [model category](c:model-category) $M$ that is [cofibrantly generated](c:cofibrantly-generated-model-category) by sets $I$ and $J$ of morphisms.
Add one condition: the underlying category of $M$ is [locally presentable](c:locally-presentable-category).
Then every object is small, so the small object argument runs for $I$ and $J$ without extra assumptions.
links.why: It shows that the only extra condition is local presentability, and that this makes the generation argument work.

reminder: A compact map is a continuous map whose image has compact closure.
definition: A [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is compact if the closure of $f(X)$ is [compact](c:compact-space), that is, if $f(X)$ is relatively compact. For a map defined on a subset of a normed space, one often asks instead that $f$ sends every bounded set to a relatively compact set.
examples: Every continuous map from a [compact space](c:compact-space) to a Hausdorff space is compact, because its image is compact.
A continuous map into a closed ball of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact, because the ball is compact.
A [compact operator](c:compact-operator) between Banach spaces sends bounded sets to relatively compact sets, so it is compact in the bounded-set sense.
Non-example: the identity map of the closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is continuous but not compact, because that ball is not compact.

steps: Take a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) $T:X\to Y$ between normed spaces, so $T$ maps the unit ball to a relatively compact set.
By linearity, $T$ maps each ball $rB$ to the relatively compact set $rT(B)$, so it maps every bounded set to a relatively compact set.
A compact operator is bounded, so it is continuous.
So $T$ is a compact map in the bounded-set sense.
links.why: It shows that a compact map is the nonlinear version of a compact operator, which is the setting of fixed point theorems such as Schauder's.

reminder: A compact self-adjoint operator is a compact operator $T$ on a Hilbert space with $T=T^*$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). A bounded operator $T:H\to H$ is a compact self-adjoint operator if $T$ is [compact](c:compact-operator), so it maps the unit ball to a relatively compact set, and [self-adjoint](c:self-adjoint-operator), so $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y$. Such an operator is diagonalizable: $H$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and the nonzero eigenvalues are real and can only accumulate at $0$.
examples: A real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix is a compact self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb R^n$ or $\mathbb C^n$.
The diagonal operator $(x_n)\mapsto(\lambda_nx_n)$ on $\ell^2$ with real numbers $\lambda_n\to0$.
The integral operator $(Tf)(x)=\int_0^1k(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ on $L^2[0,1]$ with a continuous real kernel that satisfies $k(x,y)=k(y,x)$.
Non-example: the identity of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is self-adjoint but not compact, and the Volterra operator $(Tf)(x)=\int_0^xf(y)\,dy$ is compact but not self-adjoint.

steps: Take a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) $T$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$.
Add the condition $T=T^*$, that is, $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
Then $T$ is a compact self-adjoint operator, and the spectral theorem for such operators applies.
links.why: It shows what self-adjointness adds: real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

steps: Take a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) $T$ on a Hilbert space $H$, so $T=T^*$.
Add the condition that $T$ maps the unit ball to a relatively compact set.
Then $T$ is a compact self-adjoint operator, and its spectrum is a sequence of eigenvalues that tends to $0$, together with $0$ itself.
links.why: It shows what compactness adds: the spectrum becomes discrete away from $0$.

reminder: A triangulated category with coproducts is compactly generated when a set of compact objects detects every nonzero object.
definition: Let $\mathcal T$ be a [triangulated category](c:triangulated-category) with arbitrary [coproducts](c:coproduct). It is compactly generated if there is a set $\mathcal G$ of [compact objects](c:compact-object) such that every object $X$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\Sigma^ng,X)=0$ for all $g\in\mathcal G$ and all $n\in\mathbb Z$ is zero. Equivalently, $\mathcal G$ generates $\mathcal T$ as a [localizing subcategory](c:localizing-subcategory).
examples: The [derived category](c:derived-category) $D(R)$ of a ring $R$ is compactly generated by the single compact object $R$.
The [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) is compactly generated by the sphere spectrum.
For a quasi-compact separated scheme $X$, the derived category of complexes with quasi-coherent cohomology is compactly generated.
Non-example: the bounded derived category $D^b(\mathrm{mod}\,k)$ of finite-dimensional vector spaces has no infinite coproducts, so it is not compactly generated.

steps: A [well-generated triangulated category](c:well-generated-triangulated-category) has a set of $\alpha$-small generators for some regular cardinal $\alpha$.
Choose the regular cardinal $\alpha=\aleph_0$ in this definition.
The $\aleph_0$-small objects are the compact objects, so the generators are compact.
So a compactly generated triangulated category is the well-generated case with $\alpha=\aleph_0$.
links.why: It tells a learner that compact generation is the simplest case, and that results for well-generated categories apply to it.

reminder: A compactly supported mapping space contains the maps from $X$ to a pointed space $Y$ that equal the basepoint outside a compact set.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and let $Y$ be a [pointed topological space](c:pointed-topological-space) with basepoint $y_0$. A map $f:X\to Y$ has [compact support](c:compact-support) if $f(x)=y_0$ for all $x$ outside some compact subset of $X$. The compactly supported mapping space $\mathrm{Map}_c(X,Y)$ is the subspace of the mapping space, with the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology), of the continuous maps with compact support.
examples: For $Y=\mathbb R$ pointed at $0$, the space $\mathrm{Map}_c(X,\mathbb R)$ is the space $C_c(X)$ of compactly supported real functions.

For $X=\mathbb R^n$, the maps in $\mathrm{Map}_c(\mathbb R^n,Y)$ are the pointed maps $S^n\to Y$ that equal the basepoint near $\infty$, so this space is a variant of the $n$-fold loop space $\Omega^nY$.
If $X$ is compact, every map has compact support, so $\mathrm{Map}_c(X,Y)=\mathrm{Map}(X,Y)$.
Non-example: the constant function $1$ on $\mathbb R$, with $\mathbb R$ pointed at $0$, has support all of $\mathbb R$, so it is not in $\mathrm{Map}_c(\mathbb R,\mathbb R)$.

reminder: A complete Boolean algebra is a Boolean algebra in which every subset has a supremum.
definition: A [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$ is complete if it is a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice): every subset $S\subseteq B$ has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) $\bigvee S$ and a greatest lower bound $\bigwedge S$. Complement then gives the infinite De Morgan laws $\neg\bigvee S=\bigwedge\{\neg s:s\in S\}$.
examples: The [power set](c:power-set) $\mathcal P(X)$ of any set is a complete Boolean algebra, with unions as joins and intersections as meets.
The regular open sets of a topological space form a complete Boolean algebra, where the join of a family is the interior of the closure of its union.
The [measure algebra](c:measure-algebra) of a probability space, the measurable sets modulo null sets, is a complete Boolean algebra.

Non-example: the finite-cofinite algebra of subsets of $\mathbb N$ is not complete, because $\{0\},\{2\},\{4\},\dots$ has no least upper bound: every upper bound is cofinite and loses an odd number to give a smaller upper bound.

steps: Take a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice) $L$, where every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.
Add the Boolean structure: $L$ is distributive and every element has a complement.
Then $L$ is a complete Boolean algebra, and its lattice homomorphisms preserve complements automatically.
links.why: It shows that a complete Boolean algebra is a complete lattice with distributivity and complements added.

steps: Take a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$, which has finite joins and meets and complements.
Add the condition that every subset of $B$ has a least upper bound.
A greatest lower bound then exists too, because $\bigwedge S=\neg\bigvee\{\neg s:s\in S\}$.
So $B$ is a complete Boolean algebra.
links.why: It shows that completeness needs only joins of arbitrary subsets, because complements turn them into meets.

reminder: A complete equipartite subgraph of $G$ is $r$ vertex sets of size $t$ in which vertices of distinct sets are adjacent.
definition: Let $G$ be a [graph](c:graph) with vertex set $V$ and let $r,t\ge1$. A complete equipartite subgraph of $G$ with $r$ parts of size $t$ is a collection of $r$ subsets $V_1,\dots,V_r\subseteq V$, each with $t$ elements, such that $u\in V_i$ and $v\in V_j$ are adjacent whenever $i\ne j$. The parts are then pairwise disjoint, and $G$ contains the complete multipartite graph with $r$ parts of size $t$ as a subgraph.
examples: For $r=2$ it is a complete bipartite subgraph $K_{t,t}$, and for $t=2$ it is a $4$-cycle.
For $t=1$ the parts are single vertices, so it is a [clique](c:clique) with $r$ vertices.
In the complete graph $K_6$, splitting the six vertices into three pairs gives a complete equipartite subgraph with $r=3$ and $t=2$.
Non-example: the $5$-cycle has no complete equipartite subgraph with $r=t=2$, because $K_{2,2}$ is a $4$-cycle and the $5$-cycle contains none.

steps: Take a [clique](c:clique) of $r$ vertices $v_1,\dots,v_r$ in $G$, so any two distinct vertices are adjacent.
Let the parts be the singletons $V_i=\{v_i\}$, each of size $t=1$.
Vertices in distinct parts are distinct vertices of the clique, so they are adjacent.
So the clique is a complete equipartite subgraph with $r$ parts of size $1$.
links.why: It shows that cliques are the case $t=1$, so results about cliques are the first case of results about these subgraphs.

reminder: Complex interpolation builds a Banach space between two compatible Banach spaces from analytic functions on a strip.
definition: Let $(X_0,X_1)$ be a compatible couple of [Banach spaces](c:banach-space), that is, both embed continuously in one Hausdorff topological vector space, and let $0<\theta<1$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of bounded continuous functions $f$ on the strip $0\le\operatorname{Re}z\le1$ with values in $X_0+X_1$ that are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) inside the strip, such that $t\mapsto f(it)$ is bounded and continuous into $X_0$ and $t\mapsto f(1+it)$ is bounded and continuous into $X_1$. The interpolation space is $[X_0,X_1]_\theta=\{f(\theta):f\in\mathcal F\}$ with the norm $\inf_f\max\{\sup_t\|f(it)\|_{X_0},\sup_t\|f(1+it)\|_{X_1}\}$.
examples: For $L^{p_0}$ and $L^{p_1}$ on a measure space, $[L^{p_0},L^{p_1}]_\theta=L^p$ with $\frac1p=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac{\theta}{p_1}$, which is the engine of the Riesz-Thorin theorem.
If $T$ is bounded from $X_j$ to $Y_j$ with norm $M_j$ for $j=0,1$, then $T$ is bounded from $[X_0,X_1]_\theta$ to $[Y_0,Y_1]_\theta$ with norm at most $M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^{\theta}$.

Non-example: the real $K$-method $(X_0,X_1)_{\theta,q}$ also gives intermediate spaces, but it splits elements as $x=x_0+x_1$ and does not use analytic functions on a strip, so it is not complex interpolation.

reminder: The complex roots of a polynomial $p$ are the complex numbers $z$ with $p(z)=0$.
definition: Let $p$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [complex](c:complex-number) coefficients. A complex root of $p$ is a number $r\in\mathbb C$ with $p(r)=0$, and its multiplicity is the largest $m$ such that $(z-r)^m$ divides $p(z)$. A nonzero polynomial of degree $d$ has exactly $d$ complex roots when we count multiplicity.
examples: The polynomial $z^2+1$ has the complex roots $i$ and $-i$ and no real roots.
The roots of $z^n-1$ are the $n$ [roots of unity](c:roots-of-unity) $e^{2\pi ik/n}$.
The polynomial $(z-1)^2$ has the single root $1$ with multiplicity $2$.
Non-example: $2$ is not a complex root of $z^2-1$, because $2^2-1=3\ne0$.

steps: A [root of a polynomial](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $p$ is a value $r$ in the coefficient field with $p(r)=0$.
Take the field of complex numbers as the coefficient field.
The roots are then the complex numbers $r$ with $p(r)=0$, and there are $\deg p$ of them with multiplicity.
links.why: It shows that complex roots are ordinary roots over the field $\mathbb C$, where the fundamental theorem of algebra counts them exactly.

reminder: A complexity class is a set of problems that an algorithm can solve within a given resource bound.
definition: Fix a model of computation, such as a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine), and a resource such as time or space. A complexity class is the set of decision problems that some [algorithm](c:algorithm) of that model solves within a given bound on the resource, and the kind of machine (deterministic, nondeterministic or quantum) is part of the definition.
examples: P is the class of decision problems that a deterministic Turing machine solves in polynomial time.
NP is the class of decision problems whose yes-answers have certificates that a machine can check in polynomial time.
[BQP](c:bqp) is the class of decision problems that a quantum computer solves in polynomial time with bounded error.
Non-example: a single problem such as SAT is not a complexity class; it is an element of classes such as NP.

reminder: A composition algebra is a unital algebra with a nondegenerate quadratic form $N$ such that $N(xy)=N(x)N(y)$.
definition: A composition algebra over a [field](c:field) $k$ is a finite-dimensional unital, not necessarily associative, [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) $A$ with a nondegenerate [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $N:A\to k$, the norm, such that $N(xy)=N(x)N(y)$ for all $x,y\in A$. Its dimension is $1$, $2$, $4$ or $8$ (Hurwitz's theorem), and it is associative when the dimension is at most $4$.
examples: The real numbers, the complex numbers, the [quaternions](c:quaternion) and the [octonions](c:octonion) with $N(x)=|x|^2$ are composition algebras of dimensions $1,2,4,8$.
The algebra $M_2(k)$ of $2\times2$ matrices with $N=\det$ is a composition algebra, the split quaternions.
The algebra $k\times k$ with componentwise product and $N(a,b)=ab$ is a composition algebra of dimension $2$.
Non-example: $\mathbb R^3$ with componentwise product and $N(x)=|x|^2$ is not a composition algebra, because for $x=(1,1,0)$ and $y=(0,1,1)$ we get $N(xy)=1\ne4=N(x)N(y)$.

steps: Take a real [normed division algebra](c:normed-division-algebra) $A$ whose norm $|x|$ comes from an inner product.
Then $N(x)=|x|^2$ is a positive definite quadratic form, so it is nondegenerate.
Squaring the rule $|xy|=|x||y|$ gives $N(xy)=N(x)N(y)$.
So $A$ is a composition algebra over $\mathbb R$, and the converse fails because $M_2(\mathbb R)$ with $\det$ has zero divisors.
links.why: It shows that composition algebras cover the real division algebras and also their split forms, which have zero divisors.

reminder: The composition $g\circ f$ of $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ applies $f$ first and then $g$.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ be [functions](c:function). Their composition is the function $g\circ f:X\to Z$ with $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. Composition is associative, $h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f$, and the identity function is a unit: $f\circ\mathrm{id}=f=\mathrm{id}\circ f$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$ and $g=\sin$ we have $(g\circ f)(x)=\sin(x^2)$ and $(f\circ g)(x)=\sin^2x$, so the order matters.
The chain rule gives $(g\circ f)'(x)=g'(f(x))\,f'(x)$ for differentiable $f$ and $g$.
A function and its inverse compose to the identity: $f^{-1}\circ f=\mathrm{id}_X$.
Non-example: the square root composed with $x\mapsto-x^2-1$ is undefined on $\mathbb R$, because the values of the inner function lie outside the domain $[0,\infty)$ of the outer function.

steps: Take the [category](c:category) of sets, whose objects are sets and whose morphisms are functions.
Composition of morphisms $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$ in it gives a morphism $g\circ f:x\to z$.
In this category $g\circ f$ is the function $x\mapsto g(f(x))$.
links.why: It shows that composition of functions is composition of morphisms in the category of sets, so category-theoretic facts apply.

reminder: A congruence relation is an equivalence relation that is compatible with multiplication.
definition: Let $M$ be a [magma](c:magma), a set with a [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\cdot$. A congruence relation on $M$ is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) $\sim$ such that $a\sim b$ and $c\sim d$ imply $a\cdot c\sim b\cdot d$. Then the operation is well defined on the set of classes $M/{\sim}$, and the quotient map is a homomorphism.
examples: Congruence modulo $n$ is a congruence relation on $(\mathbb Z,\cdot)$ and on $(\mathbb Z,+)$.
For a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) $\varphi:M\to N$, the relation $a\sim b\iff\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)$ is a congruence, called its [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism).
On a group, the relation $a\sim b\iff ab^{-1}\in N$ for a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) $N$ is a congruence.
Non-example: on $(\mathbb N,\cdot)$ the equivalence relation that identifies only $1$ and $2$ is not a congruence, because $1\sim2$ but $1\cdot3=3\not\sim6=2\cdot3$.

steps: Take an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) $\sim$ on a set $M$ with a [binary operation](c:binary-operation).
Add the compatibility condition: $a\sim b$ and $c\sim d$ imply $ac\sim bd$.
Then $\sim$ is a congruence relation, and the operation descends to the set of classes.
links.why: It shows that a congruence is exactly an equivalence relation that lets us form a quotient with the same operation.

reminder: A function is concave on an interval when every chord of its graph lies on or below the graph.
definition: A function $f:I\to\mathbb R$ on an [interval](c:interval) $I$ is concave if $f(tx+(1-t)y)\ge tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in I$ and $t\in[0,1]$. Equivalently, $-f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function), and a twice differentiable $f$ is concave exactly when its [second derivative](c:second-derivative) is at most $0$ on $I$.
examples: $\sin x$ is concave on $[0,\pi]$, because $(\sin x)''=-\sin x\le0$ there, and this gives Jordan's inequality $\sin x\ge2x/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$.
The functions $\log x$ and $\sqrt x$ are concave on $(0,\infty)$.
Every affine function $ax+b$ is concave, and it is also convex.
Non-example: $\sin x$ is not concave on $[0,2\pi]$, because $(\sin x)''>0$ on $(\pi,2\pi)$, so chords there lie above the graph.

reminder: The condition number $\kappa(A)=\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|$ measures how much solutions of $Ax=b$ can change under small perturbations.
definition: For an invertible [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ and a [matrix norm](c:matrix-norm) $\|\cdot\|$ induced by a vector norm, the condition number is $\kappa(A)=\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|$, and $\kappa(A)=\infty$ if $A$ is singular. In the Euclidean norm, $\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)$, the ratio of the largest and smallest singular values. If $Ax=b$ and $A(x+\delta x)=b+\delta b$, then $\|\delta x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa(A)\,\|\delta b\|/\|b\|$.
examples: The identity matrix and every orthogonal matrix have $\kappa_2=1$, the smallest possible value.
The matrix $A=\mathrm{diag}(1,10^{-6})$ has $\kappa_2(A)=10^6$, so small errors in $b$ can grow by a factor of a million in $x$.
For a [diagonalizable matrix](c:diagonalizable-matrix) $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$, every [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $A+E$ lies within $\kappa(V)\|E\|$ of an eigenvalue of $A$ (Bauer-Fike).
Non-example: the determinant does not measure conditioning, because $\mathrm{diag}(10^{-3},10^{-3})$ has determinant $10^{-6}$ but condition number $1$.

reminder: A series is conditionally convergent when it converges but the series of absolute values diverges.
definition: A [series](c:series) $\sum_na_n$ of real numbers is conditionally convergent if the sequence of [partial sums](c:partial-sum) has a finite limit but the series $\sum_n|a_n|$ diverges. Equivalently, the series converges but does not converge [absolutely](c:absolute-convergence).
examples: The alternating harmonic series $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}/n$ converges to $\ln2$, while $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n$ diverges.
The [alternating series](c:alternating-series) $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^n/\sqrt n$ converges by the alternating series test, while $\sum_{n\ge1}1/\sqrt n$ diverges.
By the Riemann series theorem, a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any real number, or to diverge.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^n/n^2$ converges absolutely and $\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n$ diverges, so neither one is conditionally convergent.

reminder: The conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X=x$ is the distribution of $Y$ after we learn that $X$ has the value $x$.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [random variables](c:random-variable). A conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ is a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) $\mu(x,B)$ such that $B\mapsto\mu(x,B)$ is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) for each $x$ and $P(X\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_A\mu(x,B)\,P_X(dx)$ for all measurable $A$ and $B$. It is unique up to a set of values $x$ of probability zero.
examples: For discrete $X,Y$ with $P(X=x)>0$, it is $P(Y=y\mid X=x)=P(X=x,Y=y)/P(X=x)$.

If $(X,Y)$ is bivariate [normal](c:normal-distribution) with correlation $\rho$ and standard deviations $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y$, then $Y\mid X=x$ is normal with mean $\mu_Y+\rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x-\mu_X)$ and variance $(1-\rho^2)\sigma_Y^2$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are [independent](c:independence), the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X=x$ is the [marginal distribution](c:marginal-distribution) of $Y$ for every $x$.
Non-example: for continuous $X$ the ratio $P(Y\in B,X=x)/P(X=x)$ is $0/0$, so it does not define the conditional distribution; the kernel and its integral identity do.

steps: Take an event $E$ with $0<P(E)<1$ and let $X=\mathbf 1_E$ be its indicator.
Define $\mu(1,B)=P(Y\in B\mid E)$ and $\mu(0,B)=P(Y\in B\mid E^c)$ by elementary [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability).
Then $P(X\in A,Y\in B)=\int_A\mu(x,B)\,P_X(dx)$ holds by the formula $P(E\cap F)=P(F\mid E)P(E)$.
So elementary conditional probability given $E$ is the conditional distribution given $X=1$.
links.why: It shows that the kernel definition extends the formula $P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ to conditioning on events of probability zero, such as $X=x$ for continuous $X$.

reminder: A confidence interval is a random interval that covers the true parameter with at least a stated probability.
definition: Let data $X$ come from a distribution $P_\theta$ with an unknown parameter $\theta$, and let $0<\alpha<1$. A $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval is a pair of [statistics](c:statistic) $L(X)\le U(X)$ such that $P_\theta\big(L(X)\le\theta\le U(X)\big)\ge1-\alpha$ for every value of $\theta$. The [probability](c:probability) refers to repeated sampling: the interval is random and $\theta$ is fixed.
examples: For a sample of size $n$ from a normal distribution with known variance $\sigma^2$, $\bar x\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ is a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval for the mean.
With unknown variance, $\bar x\pm t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\,s/\sqrt n$ is a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval for the mean of a normal sample.
Non-example: $\bar x\pm\sigma/\sqrt n$ is not a $95\%$ confidence interval for a normal mean, because its coverage is only about $68\%$.
Non-example: a $95\%$ Bayesian credible interval is a posterior statement about $\theta$, and it need not have $95\%$ coverage for every $\theta$.

reminder: A conformal block is a solution of the chiral Ward identities of a conformal field theory on a surface with marked points.
definition: In a [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) with [chiral algebra](c:chiral-algebra) $V$, take a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) $\Sigma$ with marked points $p_1,\dots,p_k$ labelled by $V$-modules $M_1,\dots,M_k$. The space of conformal blocks is the space of linear functionals on $M_1\otimes\cdots\otimes M_k$ that are invariant under the fields of $V$ that are holomorphic on $\Sigma$ minus the marked points. As $\Sigma$ moves in its [moduli space](c:moduli-space), these spaces form a vector bundle with a projectively flat connection, which is the data of a [modular functor](c:modular-functor).
examples: On the sphere with three marked points in a rational theory, the dimension of the space of conformal blocks is the fusion coefficient $N_{ijk}$ of the three labels.
For the Virasoro algebra, a four-point conformal block on the sphere is, after a standard prefactor, a function of the cross-ratio of the four marked points.
Non-example: a full correlation function of the theory is not a single conformal block; it is a single-valued combination of products of holomorphic and antiholomorphic blocks.

reminder: Two figures are congruent when a rigid motion maps one onto the other.
definition: Two figures in the Euclidean plane or space are congruent if an [isometry](c:isometry), that is, a [rigid motion](c:rigid-motion) possibly combined with a reflection, maps one onto the other. For [triangles](c:triangle) this holds exactly when the corresponding sides are equal and the corresponding [angles](c:angle) are equal, and the SSS, SAS and ASA criteria give shorter tests.
examples: Two triangles that both have sides $3$, $4$ and $5$ are congruent by the SSS criterion.
A figure and its mirror image are congruent, through a reflection.
Any two circles of the same radius are congruent.
Non-example: the triangles with sides $3,4,5$ and $6,8,10$ have equal angles but unequal sides, so they are similar but not congruent.

steps: Take two triangles whose corresponding sides are equal and whose corresponding angles are equal.
Their corresponding angles are equal, so they are [similar triangles](c:similar-triangles).
Their corresponding sides are proportional with ratio $1$.
So congruent triangles are exactly the similar triangles with ratio $1$.
links.why: It shows that congruence is similarity with the scale fixed at $1$, so similarity results apply to congruent figures.

reminder: A connecting homomorphism sends a homology class of the quotient complex to a class of the subcomplex one degree lower.
definition: Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be a [short exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex). The connecting homomorphism $\delta:H_n(C)\to H_{n-1}(A)$ sends the class of a [cycle](c:cycle) $c\in C_n$ to the class of $a\in A_{n-1}$, where $b\in B_n$ is any lift of $c$ and $\partial b$ is the image of $a$. It is a well defined [homomorphism](c:homomorphism), and it makes the sequence $\cdots\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A)\to H_{n-1}(B)\to\cdots$ exact.
examples: For $0\to\mathbb Z/2\to\mathbb Z/4\to\mathbb Z/2\to0$ applied to singular chains, $\delta$ is the [Bockstein homomorphism](c:bockstein-homomorphism) $H_n(X;\mathbb Z/2)\to H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb Z/2)$.
For $X=U\cup V$, the sequence $0\to C(U\cap V)\to C(U)\oplus C(V)\to C(U+V)\to0$ gives the boundary map $H_n(X)\to H_{n-1}(U\cap V)$ of the [Mayer-Vietoris sequence](c:mayer-vietoris-sequence).
In the snake lemma for a diagram with exact rows, the map from the kernel of the right vertical map to the cokernel of the left one is a connecting homomorphism.
Non-example: the map $H_n(B)\to H_n(C)$ induced by $B\to C$ is not a connecting homomorphism, because it keeps the degree $n$ while $\delta$ lowers it to $n-1$.

steps: Take the exact sequence of coefficient groups $0\to\mathbb Z/p\to\mathbb Z/p^2\to\mathbb Z/p\to0$.
Tensor it with the free singular chain complex of $X$ to get a short exact sequence of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex).
Its connecting homomorphism $H_n(X;\mathbb Z/p)\to H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb Z/p)$ is the [Bockstein homomorphism](c:bockstein-homomorphism).
So the Bockstein homomorphism is a special case of a connecting homomorphism.
links.why: It shows that the Bockstein homomorphism needs no new construction: it is the connecting map of a coefficient sequence.
